reason: The forward argument proves both divisibility conditions needed for the exact order. The converse repairs the supplied proof’s incorrect claim that \(-a\) has order \(p-1\): its assumed order is \((p-1)/2\), and multiplying this odd-order element by \(-1\) gives order \(p-1\).
text:
Let \(m=(p-1)/2=2t+1\), which is odd.

Suppose first that \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\). Then \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1=2m\). Hence \(a^m\) has order \(2\), so \(a^m\equiv-1\pmod p\). Therefore
\[
(-a)^m=(-1)^m a^m\equiv(-1)(-1)\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)\mid m\). Conversely, if \((-a)^n\equiv1\pmod p\), then
\[
a^{2n}=(-a)^{2n}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
Since \(a\) has order \(2m\), this implies \(2m\mid2n\), hence \(m\mid n\). Consequently \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m=(p-1)/2\).

Conversely, suppose \(\operatorname{ord}_p(-a)=m\). Put \(x=-a\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(x\) has odd order \(m\), while \(-1\) has order \(2\). These two orders are coprime. Because \(a=-x\), the commuting elements \(-1\) and \(x\) have product of order
\[
\operatorname{lcm}(2,m)=2m=p-1.
\]
Thus \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\), so \(a\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).
